newsitem.title: USA: May home sales rose, durables orders fell.
newsitem.headline: May home sales rose, durables orders fell.

text.p: Sales of existing homes rose briskly in May while orders for costly manufactured goods weakened, reports said on Wednesday, underlining the economy's slow but steady growth in the second quarter.
The National Association of Realtors said sales of previously owned homes climbed 4.4 percent last month to an annual rate of 4.24 million, despite firmer prices and slightly higher mortgage rates.

Separately, the Commerce Department said orders for long-lasting durable goods like cars and refrigerators fell 0.6 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted $176.1 billion after a revised 1.8 percent jump in April.

The data will be eyed by Federal Reserve policy-makers who meet next week to weigh their next move on interest rates. Analysts said it was likely the central bank would hold rates steady, counting on slower economic growth that will not fuel inflation.

"This only reinforces the argument that the Federal Reserve will keep monetary policy steady," said John Lonski, chief economist at Moody's Investors Service Inc. in New York. The central bank raised rates in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation.

The drop in durable goods orders was broad-based, with most major product categories aside from electrical goods posting declines. It followed a revised increase in April orders that had been reported as a smaller 1.3 percent gain.
The home sales report showed that a solid job market and steady income gains fuelled consumer optimism and persuaded many to commit to mortgages, keeping the housing market healthy.

"Given the robust activity earlier this year, we had expected sales to ease off, but the current volume reflects sustained consumer confidence, strong employment figures and some pent-up demand in the trade-up market," said Russell Booth, president of the real estate agents' group.
Existing home sales in May were the strongest since the 4.28-million annual rate a year earlier, in May 1996.

Analysts said the reports -- both of which were contrary to expectations -- buttressed the impression that the economy was slowing from its rapid 5.8 percent rate of growth in the first quarter, but still growing solidly.

"It's a clear sign there was a significant moderation in economic growth in the second quarter, perhaps to about a 2 percent annual rate," said economist Cheryl Katz of Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc. in New York, commenting on the durable goods report.

In its report, the Commerce Department said transportation orders fell 3.3 percent in May after a 2.8 percent April rise. It was the third decline in transportation orders in the past four months and the department said it was due to declines for both motor vehicles and parts and for aircraft and parts.
Transportation goods account for about a fifth of total durable goods orders. Excluding transportation, durables orders rose a slim 0.2 percent in May after a 1.6 percent April gain.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indicator of business expansion plans, rose 0.7 percent last month after falling 1.7 percent in April.

Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, fell 1.2 percent in May after rising 1.3 percent in April. It was the first month since last December that fewer finished products left the factory gate.
Unfilled orders were flat last month after two straight monthly declines.

The pickup in home sales came despite a rise in 30-year mortgage rates to an average 7.94 percent in May from 7.92 percent in April, still attractive by historical standards and lower than the 8.07 percent rate offered a year earlier.
